original_question: Which CYP enzyme, important in toluene metabolism and located on chromosome 15, is involved in the metabolism of xenobiotics in the human body?

final_qi.question: Which CYP enzyme, important in toluene metabolism and located on chromosome 15, is involved in the metabolism of xenobiotics in the human body?
final_qi.search_keyword: CYP enzyme toluene metabolism chromosome 15 xenobiotics
final_qi.long_answer: CYP1A2 is a cytochrome P450 enzyme that plays a key role in the metabolism of xenobiotics, including toluene. It is one of the enzymes involved in transforming foreign compounds into metabolites that the body can more easily eliminate. Unlike some P450 enzymes such as CYP2E1—which is also important in toluene metabolism but is located on a different chromosome—CYP1A2 is encoded by a gene on chromosome 15. This gene location is a distinguishing feature that, along with its metabolic activities in the liver, makes CYP1A2 particularly significant in both drug metabolism and the processing of environmental chemicals.

- Wikipedia: Information about: CYP2E1
Section: Introduction
Cytochrome P450 2E1 (abbreviated CYP2E1, EC 1.14.13.n7)The chemical formula is:C2636H4053O709N691S20Fe[5]. is a member of the cytochrome P450 mixed-function oxidase system, which is involved in the metabolism of xenobiotics in the body. This class of enzymes is divided up into a number of subcategories, including CYP1, CYP2, and CYP3, which as a group are largely responsible for the breakdown of foreign compounds in mammals.[6] While CYP2E1 itself carries out a relatively low number of these reactions (~4% of known P450-mediated drug oxidations), it and related enzymes CYP1A2 and CYP3A4 are responsible for the breakdown of many toxic environmental chemicals and carcinogens that enter the body, in addition to basic metabolic reactions such as fatty acid oxidations.[7]
Section: Regulation
In humans, the CYP2E1 enzyme is encoded by the CYP2E1 gene.[28] The enzyme has been identified in fetal liver, where it is posited to be the predominant ethanol-metabolizing enzyme, and may be connected to ethanol-mediated teratogenesis.[29] In rats, within one day of birth the hepatic CYP2E1 gene is activated transcriptionally. CYP2E1 expression is easily inducible, and can occur in the presence of a number of its substrates, including ethanol,[23] isoniazid,[23] tobacco,[30] isopropanol,[7] benzene,[7] toluene,[7] and acetone.[7] For ethanol specifically, it seems that there exist two stages of induction, a post-translational mechanism for increased protein stability at low levels of ethanol and an additional transcriptional induction at high levels of ethanol.[31]
Section: Disease relevance
CYP2E1 is expressed in high levels in the liver, where it works to clear toxins from the body.[9][10] In doing so, CYP2E1 bioactivates a variety of common anesthetics, including paracetamol (acetaminophen), halothane, enflurane, and isoflurane.[7] The oxidation of these molecules by CYP2E1 can produce harmful substances such as trifluoroacetic acid chloride from halothane [32] or NAPQI from paracetamol (acetaminophen) and is a major reason for their observed hepatotoxicity in patients. CYP2E1 and other cytochrome P450 enzymes can inadvertently produce reactive oxygen species (ROS) in their active site when catalysis is not coordinated correctly, resulting in potential lipid peroxidation as well as protein and DNA oxidation.[15] CYP2E1 is particularly susceptible to this phenomenon compared to other P450 enzymes, suggesting that its expression levels may be important for negative physiological effects observed in a number of disease states.[15] CYP2E1 expression levels have been correlated with a variety of dietary and physiological factors, such as ethanol consumption,[33] diabetes,[34] fasting,[35] and obesity.[36] It appears that cellular levels of the enzyme may be controlled by the molecular chaperone HSP90, which upon association with CYP2E1 allows for transport to the proteasome and subsequent degradation. Ethanol and other substrates may disrupt this association, leading to the higher expression levels observed in their presence.[37] The increased expression of CYP2E1 accompanying these health conditions may therefore contribute to their pathogenesis by increasing the rate of production of ROS in the body.[15]
